title: Major outages are causing concern and confusion. Gen can help.
summary: Outages at the FAA, United Airlines, Apple, and several banks have left people feeling uneasy. Gen’s family of brands can help bring peace of mind as outages, breaches and scams surge
body_markdown:
Several major services recently went down within a few days of each other, leaving people unable to email, fly, or log in to their bank accounts. The outages themselves were not cyberattacks, according to the companies involved. But when people can’t reach the services they most depend on, the confusion can create concern. Or even an opening for scammers posing as banks, airlines, tech companies, or customer support.


And although these outages are not confirmed cyber incidents, in the past weeks we’ve seen an influx of breaches and attacks that add to these feelings. At Gen, our family of brands help people stay more informed, protected and in control when digital disruptions and online threats feel closer to home. The recent disruptions show how quickly a technical problem at one company can ripple into people’s everyday lives, while creating opportunities for impersonation and fraud. Major U.S. services experience outages within days


Between November 12 and November 16, outages disrupted several major companies and services that many consumers rely on.


- **November 12, Microsoft 365:** Outlook, Teams, SharePoint, and Copilot were disrupted for hours.[Microsoft](https://x.com/Microsoft/status/2121282013600907325?a=prw-goG0it6s5Tc6Pow&s=20) said the outage was not the result of a cyberattack and restored services gradually.
- **November 13, FAA:** The[FAA](https://www.faa.gov/newsroom/nationwide-ground-stop-questions-and-answers) issued a nationwide ground stop on departing flights after a telecommunications outage affected air traffic control centers. The FAA lifted the stop later that day.
- **November 16, multiple U.S. banks:** Thousands of banking customers reported difficulty accessing their online accounts at several major financial institutions,[AP](https://apnews.com/article/bank-outage-chase-wells-fargo-truist-50fee2693c22f597fa6ca51a97ef2cda) reported. Chase said a software bug slowed some transactions and that the problem was technical, not cyber-related. Wells Fargo said online banking was temporarily unavailable. U.S. Bank said its systems were not directly hit.
- **November 16, United Airlines:**[United](https://x.com/united/status/2122468207202279437?a=4OaD-xydDu8ezY_IlIs&s=20) reported a system outage that delayed departing flights. It was resolved the same day. It was resolved the same day.
- **November 17, Apple:** Apple users reported problems, such as difficulties activating devices and signing in, with services like iCloud, the App Store and Apple Pay, according to[The New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/17/technology/apple-down-outage-issues.html) .


None of these incidents need to be a cyberattack to create an opportunity for cybercriminals. Scammers exploit confusion around a real-world event, impersonating affected companies and offering bogus fixes, updates, or customer support.


Separately,[researchers at Report URI](https://www.newsweek.com/cyber-attack-websites-affected-12725863) reported on November 17 that malicious software had been found on the websites of 178 organizations, including Zoom and CNN. It isn’t yet clear how many people, if any, lost information, and there is no established connection between that incident and the outages described above. ## Why major outages can create opportunities for scammers


Widespread outages like these can create opportunities for scammers, as the confusion and uncertainty around them creates a sense of urgency: People want answers and fixes quickly, which can make them less likely to pause when they receive a text or email that seems like it will give them the update they are waiting for.


Scammers borrow trust from familiar brands. The use of familiar brand names makes the bait more believable. Scam messages can look like they came from Microsoft, an airline, or a bank.


When several major outages occur within days of one another, scammers also have multiple potential scenarios to exploit. A scam might offer an Outlook mailbox fix, a flight rebooking, or bank account verification. Scammers may call pretending to be an airline or bank employee, or send an email or text with a link to restore your email or rebook your flight. They may also ask for login details for the services you are trying to reach.


This type of impersonation is a common phishing tactic.


## How outage scams can lead to identity theft


Some scammers are after a quick payday, but others may have more nefarious intentions. Confusion caused by widespread outages can open the door to identity theft.


For example, you might get an email or text from what looks like your bank or airline. Clicking on a link could lead to a fake login page. Entering your password could give a scammer access to your account. They may also use phone calls, texts, or emails related to these outages to obtain personal details such as a Social Security number, date of birth, or credit card number.


This information can be used to open new accounts or take over existing ones. Phishing scams designed to obtain passwords, account numbers, Social Security numbers, and other sensitive information can ultimately lead to identity theft.


## How to protect yourself from phishing and identity theft


When you’re frustrated or fearful, you might be more vulnerable to scammers who want to take advantage of these major disruptions. However, these are times when you should be more guarded, not less.


To help reduce your risk and better protect your money, accounts, and identity, security experts recommend following these best practices:


- **Go directly to the source:** Don’t open links in unexpected emails or texts you receive about outages. Open the official app or type in the company’s website address yourself.
- **Be wary of urgency:** Messages that say “act within 24 hours” or “your account will be locked” should give you a reason to stop and verify the message before taking action. Phishing messages commonly manufacture account problems or other urgent situations to get people to click links or provide information.
- **Verify customer support numbers:** If you want to call your bank or airline to get an update, find phone numbers on the company’s official website or the back of your credit card, not in an unexpected message or search ad.
- **Use two-factor authentication:** Two-factor authentication adds another layer of protection if a scammer obtains your username and password. Using 2FA makes it harder for scammers to access your accounts, even if they obtain your login credentials.
- **Never share one-time codes:** If you receive a verification code you didn’t request, don’t provide it to someone who unexpectedly contacts you.
- **Report suspicious messages:** Report phishing attempts to the company being impersonated and your email or phone provider. The FTC also advises consumers to report phishing attempts through ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
- **Use scam detection and identity protection tools:** Scams are becoming increasingly hard to spot. Advanced scam detection tools can help you figure out what’s real and what’s malicious, while identity protection tools can alert you to threats and help you resolve them.
